papers.title: Low-Dimensional Adaptation of Rectified Flow: A Diffusion and Stochastic Localization Perspective
papers.abstract: In recent years, Rectified flow (RF) has gained considerable popularity largely due to its generation efficiency and state-of-the-art performance. In this paper, we investigate how well RF automatically adapts to the intrinsic low dimensionality of the support of the target distribution to accelerate sampling. We show that, using a carefully designed end-point adapted time-discretization scheme and with sufficiently accurate drift estimates, the RF sampler enjoys an iteration complexity of order $O(k/\varepsilon)$ (up to log factors), where $\varepsilon$ is the precision in total variation distance and $k$ is the intrinsic dimension of the target distribution. In addition, we show that the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) procedure is equivalent to a stochastic version of RF by establishing a novel connection between these processes and stochastic localization. Building on this connection, we further design a stochastic RF sampler that also adapts to the low-dimensionality of the target distribution under mild requirements on the accuracy of the drift estimates, and also with a specific time schedule. We illustrate the efficacy of newly designed time-discretization schedules with simulations on the synthetic data and text-to-image (T2I) data experiments.

papers.title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
papers.abstract: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.

papers.title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
papers.abstract: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.

papers.title: Bounded-Order Non-Identifiability in Latent Structure Block Models: The Fiber in Closed Form
papers.abstract: A graphon is determined by all of its homomorphism densities, but motif-based methods use finitely many. We compute exactly what that truncation costs in a natural family: latent structure block models whose positions lie on $K$ rays, equivalently degree-corrected block models of rank two. For a given radial law, the configurations that agree on every graph with fewer than $2K-1$ vertices form a one-dimensional fiber, which we give in closed form with explicit endpoints; the friendship graph $F_{K-1}$ is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no fixed motif order serves every $K$. The separating signal is suppressed by a factor of at most $m_1^{2(K-1)}$, where $m_1$ is the mean squared slope, about $10^{-4}$ at $K=4$: detecting it from motif counts would take about $10^{15}$ nodes in a single graph, at any edge density. The information is nonetheless in the graph; the fiber belongs to the statistic, not the model. Common spectral pipelines, which count no motifs, still slide along the fiber by more than a third of its length at ordinary densities, with confidence regions that almost never contain the truth, while model-based fits of the same embedding do not. We give practitioners four checks: whether a fit is at risk, what to run instead, why a confidence interval will not warn, and how wide the remaining ambiguity is.

papers.title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
papers.abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

papers.title: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
papers.abstract: Stability under input perturbations is necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. Weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. However, existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are insufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. In this paper, we establish a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm product constraint. This theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth H\"{o}lder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as the network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed. We then propose a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still achieving the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, we establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and provide robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies show that the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to that of classical deep network methods.

papers.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
papers.abstract: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.

papers.title: On the parametric and semiparametric Fisher information matrix for non-zero mean stationary spherical invariant random processes
papers.abstract: The classical Whittle formula provides a closed-form expression for the asymptotic Fisher information matrix (FIM) rate of multidimensional, real-valued, zero-mean, purely nondeterministic stationary Gaussian processes (GPs), expressed in terms of their parameterized spectra within a maximum-likelihood framework. However, the Gaussian assumption underlying this result restricts its applicability to many real-world signals exhibiting heavy-tailed or non-Gaussian behavior. In this paper, we extend Whittle's result to multidimensional, real-valued stationary compound Gaussian processes (CGPs) with arbitrary mean, under a unified framework encompassing fully known, parameterized, and completely unknown density generators. Building upon the Slepian-Bangs formula for $n$ consecutive observations and extending it to the semiparametric setting, we leverage the asymptotic properties of block Toeplitz matrices to obtain a closed-form spectral-domain expression for the asymptotic FIM rate. The resulting expression, common to all density generator families, generalizes the standard zero-mean Gaussian formula by incorporating a distribution-dependent contribution associated with the nonzero mean, and an additional covariance term that is invariant to the choice of non-Gaussian distribution. This extension enables efficient and theoretically grounded performance analysis for heavy-tailed signal processing applications.

papers.title: Inference for conditional Fr\'echet means via Riemannian Robust Bias Correction
papers.abstract: We develop an intrinsic framework for inference on conditional Fr\'echet means with predictors and responses taking values in finite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. We derive a second-order expansion of the smoothing bias, represented in the tangent space via the logarithm map, and show that this bias can affect first-order inference. We propose Riemannian robust bias correction (RRBC), which estimates the leading smoothing bias using a local quadratic regression in the response tangent space and corrects the estimator through the exponential map. Our leave-one-out (LOO) covariance estimator uses intrinsic displacements between the full-sample and LOO RRBC estimates, accounting for the variability of the estimated bias correction and its covariance with the local linear estimator. We establish asymptotically valid pointwise confidence sets and simultaneous confidence tubes without undersmoothing. Simulations on spheres and symmetric positive-definite matrices show that RRBC can improve coverage when smoothing bias is nonnegligible. Cardiovascular and ocean-current applications illustrate simultaneous hypothesis testing and inference for smooth functionals.

papers.title: Minimax estimation for simultaneous deconvolution model in random design using wavelets
papers.abstract: Simultaneous deconvolution model is investigated when the design points are random and follow bounded densities and errors are either $i.i.d.$ or long-memory dependent. We propose wavelet hard-thresholding estimators, and show that they achieve asymptotically near-optimal convergence rates for the $L^2$-risk when the response function belongs to Besov space under both $i.i.d.$ errors and homoskedastic, long-memory errors. However, under heteroskedastic, long-memory errors the estimator is not optimal. For the $i.i.d.$ errors, the convergence rates are {identical} to those found in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design {and $i.i.d.$ errors}. However, for long-memory dependent errors, the convergence rates are new {and completely different from those in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design and long-memory errors}.

papers.title: Federated Differential Privacy with Batch Contamination
papers.abstract: We study mean estimation under federated differential privacy (FDP) constraints and batch contamination, considering both Gaussian and heavy-tailed distributions. In the homogeneous setting, where sample sizes and privacy budgets are constant across servers, we show that the costs of privacy and contamination disentangle. Under a bounded $v$th moment condition, with $v \in (1, \infty)$, the cost of batch contamination is of order $(\varepsilon/n)^{2-2/v}\vee \varepsilon^2/n$, where $\varepsilon$ is the contamination level and $n$ is the per-batch sample size. This reveals a phase transition at $\varepsilon\asymp n^{1-v/2}$, for $v > 2$, which is the first of its kind in the literature. We develop a two-stage procedure that achieves the minimax rate up to poly-logarithmic factors. A key component is a private smoothed voting procedure tailored to the FDP setting that provides optimal sensitivity control. For heterogeneous batch sample sizes and privacy budgets, we introduce a batch partitioning framework that groups batches with comparable per-batch sample sizes and privacy budgets. Surprisingly, the minimax rate is determined, up to poly-logarithmic factors, by the most informative group of batches. Consequently, in some regimes, it is minimax optimal to use only an arbitrarily small proportion of the data set. Heterogeneity also introduces interactions between the costs of privacy and contamination, in contrast to their disentanglement in the homogeneous setting. For unknown contamination level, we propose an adaptive, near-minimax optimal Lepski-type extension for the heterogeneous Gaussian setting, designed specifically to prevent privacy leakage by ensuring no repeated use of data points.

papers.title: Spectral Stability and Convergence of the Unnormalized Graph Laplacian on Noisy Point Clouds
papers.abstract: The first eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the unnormalized graph Laplacian of clean samples from a manifold, suitably scaled, approximate those of a weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator. However, the samples are usually observed with noise and therefore need not lie on the manifold. We build the clean and noisy graph Laplacians, with bandwidth $\varepsilon$, on the clean samples and on the noisy observations, where the noise is arbitrary but bounded by $\delta$. We show that, with high probability, the first eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the noisy graph Laplacian are close to those of the clean one: the eigenvalues within $O(\delta/\varepsilon)$, and the subspaces spanned by the first eigenvectors within $O(\sqrt{\delta/\varepsilon})$, whether or not the eigenvalues are simple. Consequently, if $\delta$ is small enough relative to $\varepsilon$, the noisy graph Laplacian approximates the weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator at the same rate as the clean one. We also show that, for large noise, we can get the same rate as the clean graph Laplacian by first using a denoiser, and then building the graph Laplacian on the denoised observations.

papers.title: Berry Esseen bounds for fractional Vasicek type processes: continuous and high-frequency regimes
papers.abstract: We study the estimation of the drift parameters $(a,b)$ of the fractional Vasicek process $dX_t=a(b-X_t)\,dt+dB^H_t$, driven by a fractional Brownian motion of Hurst index $H\in(0,1)$. The estimators are of moment type, built from the empirical mean and variance of the path, and are analysed in two regimes: continuous observation on $[0,T]$, and high-frequency observation at times $t_i=i\Delta_n$ with $\Delta_n\to0$ and $T_n=n\Delta_n\to\infty$. Using the Malliavin--Stein method on the second Wiener chaos, we prove consistency of both estimators for every $H$, and quantitative central limit theorems in the Wasserstein distance: for $H<\frac34$ for the estimator of $a$, with explicit rates depending on $H$, and for every $H\in(0,1)$ for the estimator of $b$, at the rate $T^{-H}$. In the discrete regime the bounds contain an additional discretization term of order $\Delta_n^{\min\{H+1/2,\,1\}}$, and for $H<\frac12$ the central limit theorem for the estimator of $b$ requires in addition $T_n^{1-2H}\Delta_n^{1+2H}\to0$. A short Monte Carlo study illustrates the results.

papers.title: Parameter estimation for discretely observed rough fractional interacting particle systems
papers.abstract: We study parametric inference for interacting particle systems driven by independent fractional Brownian motions, based on discrete observations of all particles over a fixed time horizon. Our goal is to estimate an unknown drift parameter in the joint limit as the number of particles increases and the observation mesh vanishes. For $H>\frac 12$, we construct contrast based estimators by extending the discrete time least squares approach of Neuenkirch and Tindel to the interacting setting. For the rough regime $H\in(\frac 14,\frac 12)$, we introduce a modified contrast and use the stochastic sewing lemma to handle the first order approximations available from discrete observations. Our analysis combines the propagation of chaos for the associated fractional McKean Vlasov equation with estimates controlling the temporal discretization error. When the Hurst parameter and the diffusion coefficient are known, we establish strong consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. The asymptotic results reveal an interplay between the number of particles and the temporal discretization: the convergence rate with respect to the observation mesh changes at $H=\frac 34$, while the asymptotic normality holds in both regimes considered. We further develop a joint estimation procedure for the drift parameter, the Hurst parameter, and the diffusion coefficient, extending quadratic-variation methods for fractional Brownian motion to the interacting particle framework. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed estimators.

papers.title: Worst-case bias of the independence assumption for functions of two ordinal variables
papers.abstract: Let ordinal grades $X$ and $Y$ be obtained by cutting a pair of random variables with copula $C$ at arbitrary thresholds, and let $g$ be a function of the grades. We study the largest error $S_C(g)$, over all thresholds, that is, over all marginal laws, made when the mean of $g(X,Y)$ is computed as if the grades were independent. This is the counterpart of the classical dependence-uncertainty problem: the copula is fixed and the discretisation is free. The error is caused entirely by the interaction of the inputs, measured by an index $\rho(g)$, the largest absolute $g$-volume of a rectangle of grades, which vanishes if and only if $g$ is additive. For every copula, $S_C(g)$ lies between $\rho(g)$ times the largest deviation of $C$ from the independence copula and $\rho(g)$ times half the total variation of their difference, and the factor one half cannot be improved. For the Gaussian copula with correlation $\lambda$ we prove that $S_C(g)$ equals $|\lambda|\rho(g)/(2\pi)$ to first order, with a sharp constant and an explicit remainder. The same first-order law holds for copula families whose first-order departure from independence is a product of unimodal factors, including the Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern, Ali-Mikhail-Haq, Frank, Clayton and Plackett families, and we characterise the Archimedean families with this property. An application to the TNM staging of colon cancer, with data from a clinical trial, compares the bounds with the actual error of the independence computation.

papers.title: Structural latent dimension: deterministic geometry and local Fisher structure
papers.abstract: We study the structural dimension of a second-order object: the minimum latent dimension that remains necessary relative to a declared class of competing dependence. Building on minimum-rank factor analysis and low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, we use distances to lower-dimensional classes to describe inference near structural ambiguity. General distance and tangent-cone facts yield confidence statements and local margins. For rank-zero competitors with bounded residual degree, we derive exact maximum-weight $b$-matching formulas, support-slack tangent cones and sparse-spike angles; a shared residual support across a field can produce separation absent pointwise. We give positive-semidefinite brackets, a dimension-free Gaussian likelihood expansion, an exact quotient by the tangent of a low-rank background, and a detection floor from the margin. Equal-angle configurations with different branch multiplicities motivate static and spectral detection conjectures. Joint low-rank/residual profiling and the sharp composite information boundaries remain open.

papers.title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
papers.abstract: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based \(e\)-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based \(e\)-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed \(e\)-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal \(e\)-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the \(1/k\) fraction of the largest \(m\)th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.

papers.title: On the Validity of Fisher Randomization Tests under the Weak Null
papers.abstract: Consider the problem of testing the Neyman weak null of no sample average treatment effect $H_{0N}:\tau = 0$ in randomized experiments with binary outcomes. Although the Fisher Randomization Test (FRT) is typically justified under Fisher's sharp null of no individual treatment effect, we show that it is finite-sample-valid for the weak null $H_{0N}$ in three common combinations of study design and test statistic: 1) balanced completely randomized experiments with the difference-in-means test statistic, 2) matched pairs experiments with the same test statistic, and 3) balanced Bernoulli randomized experiments with the centered Horvitz-Thompson test statistic. As an immediate corollary, Fisher's exact test in a balanced completely randomized experiment is valid under the weak null, and so is McNemar's test in a matched pairs experiment. Similar results hold for the one-sided null $H_0:\tau \leq 0$. Beyond balanced designs, we show that twice the one-sided FRT $p$-value with the same test statistics is valid under $H_{0N}$. In simulation experiments, the FRTs compare favorably to other exact procedures.

papers.title: Learning Robust Treatment Rules for Censored Data
papers.abstract: There is a fast-growing literature on estimating optimal treatment rules directly by maximizing the expected outcome. In biomedical studies and operations applications, censored survival outcomes are frequently observed, in which case the truncated mean survival time and survival probability are of great interest. In this paper, we propose two robust criteria for learning optimal treatment rules with censored survival outcomes; the former one targets an optimal treatment rule maximizing the truncated mean survival time, where the cutoff is specified by a given quantile such as the median; the latter one targets an optimal treatment rule maximizing buffered survival probabilities, where the predetermined threshold is adjusted to account for the truncated mean survival time. We develop a sampling-based difference-of-convex algorithm for learning the proposed optimal treatment rules, and provide theoretical justifications for them. In simulation studies, our estimators show improved performance compared to existing methods. We also demonstrate the proposed method using AIDS clinical trial data.

papers.title: Induced replication and the assessment of models
papers.abstract: The paper is a first attempt at a foundation of inference for the assessment of semiparametric and other high-dimensional models, seeking reconciliation with the low-dimensional Fisherian foundations by replacing out-of-sample prediction error as a criterion for semiparametric model assessment by a type of within-sample prediction error. We highlight the possibility, in some contexts, of avoiding the usual semiparametric considerations, including estimation of unparametrised nuisance components and the associated difficulties of tuning-parameter choice that blur the distinction between estimation and model assessment. A key aspect of the work is the inducement of replication under the postulated model, the route to which being context-specific but based on structural properties of the model. The ideas are isolated through examples.

papers.title: MIST: Reliable Streaming Decision Trees for Online Class-Incremental Learning via McDiarmid Bound
papers.abstract: Streaming decision trees are natural candidates for open-world continual learning, as they perform local updates, enjoy bounded memory, and static decision boundaries. Despite these, they still fail in online class-incremental learning due to two coupled miscalibrations: (i) their split criterion grows unreliable as the class count K expands, and (ii) the absence of knowledge transfer at split time. Both failures share a common root: the range of Information Gain intrinsically scales with log2 K. Consequently, any Hoeffding-style confidence radius derived from it must inevitably grow with the class count, making a K-independent split criterion structurally impossible, taking away the potential benefits of applying streaming decision trees to continual learning. To fix this issue, we present MIST (McDiarmid Incremental Streaming Tree), which resolves both failures through three integrated components: (i) a tight, K-independent McDiarmid confidence radius for Gini splitting that acts as a structural regulariser; (ii) a Bayesian inheritance protocol that projects parent statistics to child nodes via truncated-Gaussian moments, with variance reduction guarantees strongest precisely when splitting is most conservative; and (iii) per-leaf KLL quantile sketches that support both continuous threshold evaluation and geometry-adaptive leaf prediction from a single data structure. On standard and stress-test tabular streams, MIST is competitive with global parametric methods on near-Gaussian benchmarks and uniquely robust on non-Gaussian geometry where SOTA benchmarks collapse.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Canonical Correlation Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper studies high-dimensional canonical correlation analysis (CCA) with an emphasis on the vectors that define canonical variables. The paper shows that when two dimensions of data grow to infinity jointly and proportionally, the classical CCA procedure for estimating those vectors fails to deliver a consistent estimate. This provides the first result on the impossibility of identification of canonical variables in the CCA procedure when all dimensions are large. As a countermeasure, the paper derives the magnitude of the estimation error, which can be used in practice to assess the precision of CCA estimates. Applications of the results to cyclical vs. non-cyclical stocks and to a limestone grassland data set are provided.

papers.title: A nonparametric test for diurnal variation in spot correlation processes
papers.abstract: The association between log-price increments of exchange-traded equities, as measured by their spot correlation estimated from high-frequency data, exhibits a pronounced upward-sloping and almost piecewise linear relationship at the intraday horizon. There is notably lower-on average less positive-correlation in the morning than in the afternoon. We develop a nonparametric testing procedure to detect such variation in a correlation process. The test statistic has a known distribution under the null hypothesis, whereas it diverges under the alternative. We run a Monte Carlo simulation to discover the finite sample properties of the test statistic, which are close to the large sample predictions, even for small sample sizes and realistic levels of diurnal variation. In an application, we implement the test on a high-frequency dataset covering the stock market over an extended period. The test leads to rejection of the null most of the time. This suggests diurnal variation in the correlation process is a nontrivial effect in practice. We show how conditioning information about macroeconomic news and corporate earnings announcements affect the intraday correlation curve.

papers.title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference I
papers.abstract: Approximate Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (ALO-CV) is a method that has been proposed to estimate the generalization error of a regularized estimator in the high-dimensional regime where dimension and sample size are of the same order, the so-called ``proportional regime''. A new analysis is developed to derive the consistency of ALO-CV for non-differentiable regularizers under Gaussian covariates and strong convexity. Using a conditioning argument, the difference between the ALO-CV weights and their counterparts in mean-field inference is shown to be small. Combined with upper bounds between the mean-field inference estimate and the leave-one-out quantity, this provides a proof that ALO-CV approximates the leave-one-out quantity up to negligible error terms. Linear models with square loss, robust linear regression and single-index models are explicitly treated.

papers.title: Assessing model calibration with boosting trees
papers.abstract: The main goal in regression modelling consists in approximating the conditional mean of a response given a set of features. A regression function is said to be strongly calibrated if the resulting mean estimates match the true conditional means for almost every set of features. Aiming for strong calibration seems not achievable in practice as one typically deals with finite samples of noisy observations. A weaker notion of calibration is auto-calibration, and it means that the conditional expectation of the response, given a mean estimate, matches this estimate. This notion is important, e.g., in insurance pricing as it ensures no cross-subsidization between different price cohorts. In this paper, we show that boosting trees can be used to test necessary conditions for strong calibration and auto-calibration, respectively. The practical relevance of our approach is supported by a numerical example, in which the proposed tests achieve high empirical power.

papers.title: Nonparametric Regression on Fixed-Cardinality Subsets:Minimax Risk and Random-Design Effects
papers.abstract: We study regression from noisy evaluations of uniformly sampled subsets containing exactly \(k\) items from a ground set of size \(d\), a setting motivated by combination screening. The fixed-cardinality constraint couples membership coordinates and prevents a direct use of product-domain notions of interaction and smoothness. Using the harmonic decomposition of the Johnson graph, we define an intrinsic Johnson--Sobolev scale and determine the exact dimensions of low-order interaction spaces. We establish finite-sample risk bounds for harmonic projection and a nonasymptotic minimax characterization when the Sobolev energy budget is bounded relative to the noise variance proxy. We also study sparsity when responses depend on few items, quantifying the reduced interaction dimension and the effects of unknown support and rare configurations. When the empirical Gram matrix is well conditioned, stable least squares removes the design fluctuation of the component already in the fitted space. A rank-deficiency analysis identifies the components left unresolved by random sampling. Combined with a centered completion estimator, it yields minimax bounds matching up to constants whenever \(\min(k,d-k)\) and the smoothness order are fixed, without restricting the signal-to-noise ratio. Numerical experiments distinguish observation noise, design fluctuation, and incomplete coverage; NCI-ALMANAC drug-pair scores provide a real-data illustration.

papers.title: Semiparametric Efficient Inference under Non-Informative Complex Survey Designs
papers.abstract: Under non-informative complex survey designs, dependence among sampling indicators prevents the direct application of standard i.i.d. semiparametric efficiency theory. We introduce a \emph{reference Poisson experiment}, a hypothetical i.i.d.\ experiment constructed from the limiting inclusion probabilities of the original dependent design. Under suitable conditions, the actual observed-data experiment is in fact locally asymptotically normal, with the same tangent-space geometry as the reference Poisson experiment. Consequently, the efficient influence function derived by orthogonal projection in this hypothetical i.i.d.\ setting characterizes efficient estimators under the original dependent design. This yields a systematic approach to efficiency analysis for general semiparametric full-data models and pathwise-differentiable targets under complex survey designs. Under the joint superpopulation--design law, the efficiency bounds depend on the design only through its limiting inclusion probabilities. For finite-population targets whose first-order expansions are governed by the full-data efficient influence function, the same estimators are efficient under both superpopulation and finite-population centering, with bounds linked by a Pythagorean identity yielding a generalized finite-population correction. We establish efficiency of cross-fitted mean and conditional-mean regression estimators under explicit design-specific sufficient conditions. Simulations and California Academic Performance Index data illustrate the theory.

papers.title: Optimal Linear Functional Estimation for Proportionally High-Dimensional Linear Models
papers.abstract: We study estimation of a linear functional in random-design linear models when $\gamma=p/n \in (1, \infty)$ under the dense regime where the design covariance is unknown, and neither the regression vector nor the precision matrix is assumed sparse. Suppose the spectrum of the design covariance belongs to $[\ell,L]$, and let $\kappa=L/\ell$. We establish that the minimax mean squared error for the linear functional is of order $n^{-\alpha(\kappa,\gamma)}$, where the exponent $\alpha(\kappa,\gamma)$ has an explicit elliptic-integral representation and $\alpha(\kappa,\gamma) < 1$ when both $\kappa > 1$ and $\gamma > 1$. We propose the Bocca estimator, which combines empirically calibrated resolvents through a complex contour integral to attain the optimal rate. We also establish asymptotic normality of the Bocca estimator and develop a variance estimator for valid inference.

papers.title: Sparse Fault Detection in Linear Systems: Equivalence of GLR Tests and $\ell_1$-regularized Least Squares
papers.abstract: This paper studies the detection of an impulsive fault of unknown time and input channel in a linear system with unknown initial state and Gaussian measurement noise. First, we show that the generalized likelihood ratio test, after the initial state is eliminated by projection onto the parity space, is the zero-solution test of a weighted lasso with an unpenalized nuisance block; the regularization parameter is the test threshold, and for unknown noise variance the same holds for the square-root lasso. Second, we show that the null distribution depends on the system only through a Gram matrix, so that the threshold is computed exactly and offline, and we compare it with closed-form bounds. Third, we characterize the fraction of a fault that survives the projection: we give it in closed form through observability Gramians, we show that it converges to a geometrically decaying profile for strictly stable systems, and that, for systems with unit-modulus modes, it grows linearly with the fault time as a fraction of the record length. Numerical studies, including a two-input, two-output example, illustrate the results.

papers.title: Decomposition Bounds for MCMC with Mixture Targets: Multimodality and Heavy-Tailedness
papers.abstract: We establish quantitative mixing-time bounds for Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms targeting multimodal and heavy-tailed mixtures. The dynamics of a Markov chain are decomposed into local and global levels, and possibly weak Poincar\'{e} inequalities at both levels are combined to form convergence bounds. We apply this framework to location and scale mixtures of strongly log-concave distributions, obtaining explicit convergence bounds for random-walk Metropolis, proximal, and random-scan Gibbs samplers. For location mixtures connected along a finite path, the bounds depend polynomially on the number of components and exponentially on neighboring separation, remaining informative as the overall diameter grows. For scale mixtures, we relate the global dynamics of the chain to the isoperimetry of the log-scale mixing distribution, and illustrate the effect of heavy-tailed targets by examining inverse-gamma mixing distributions.
